title: Will English eat Japanese?
summary: A talk, not a grammar lesson: why English words enter Japanese, and why this does not change its structure.

blocks.text: This episode is a talk about vocabulary and culture, so there is no test. Its main points:

items: English words enter Japanese for the same reasons they enter other languages: English is the school language, the language of technology, and it carries prestige (cool, cute, clever).
Katakana makes loan words stand out on the page, especially to foreigners, so they seem more numerous than they are.
Loan words usually live beside native words rather than replacing them; the tiger is still 虎, though ライオン has largely replaced 獅子.
Foreign words arrive as **nouns** (you add する to make a verb), so they do not change how sentences are built.

blocks.text: A quick check from the talk: open any Japanese book and count the katakana words. Most are names or invented words, not loan words.

blocks.jp: 今日はコーヒーを飲みながらメールを送った。
blocks.en: Today I sent an email while drinking coffee.

blocks.text: The history behind the talk: Chinese words, now about sixty percent of the vocabulary, changed Japanese vocabulary but not its structure, just as French changed English vocabulary and not its structure.
